description: No title provided - The wider scientific computing industry is booming - with server sales growing, cloud usage growing, compute speeds and storage capacities growing, and demand for simulation, optimization and HPDA/AI expanding to more of the enterprise segment (as well as academic and government). At the same time, the commercial software landscape is becoming ever more difficult to navigate - as hardware vendors increasingly offer components (including libraries) for free and open source ecosystems reach an unprecedented level of maturity. The forces that shape the Numerical Libraries Industry are not benign and have changed over time. The Threat of New Entrants is High - This threat is present and continual. It has caused erosion in the past and will do so in the future, fuelled by hardware and cloud vendor rivalries, by open source contributors (academics, students and government labs, often with financial contributions from industry), and by skilled developers launching new commercial offerings. The Bargaining Power of Suppliers is Moderate What next and algorithms suppliers (academic and government collaborators, algorithm developers) offer a credible threat to forward integrate - by offering free libraries, releasing new open source libraries, or launching new commercial libraries businesses. There is, however, a large number of suppliers which reduces their overall power. The Bargaining Power of Buyers is High - They now capture a lot of the value and have come to expect much libraries content to come for free. They have an increasing selection of free open source options to choose from, and they can turn to substitutes (some of which are also free) to satisfy their needs. Customers with code-base dependencies or other specialised needs have reduced leverage. Firms must introduce features, improve performance, adapt to new technology, specialize or meet risk/regulatory requirements to differentiate. The Threat of Substitution is Moderate-High - Toolkits and readymade software (some of which are, again, free) substitute the need to build with numerical libraries. While deep learning may replace numerical libraries in certain areas, it is likely that machine learning, deep learning and traditional numerical libraries will need to work together in the future, so compatibility will become important. Rivalry Among Existing Competitors is High - Vendors are engaged in their own rivalry for dominance in shifting chip and cloud industries. Python and Julia are eroding industry value overall, challenging the competitive equilibrium of Integrated Math Engines like Mathworks, and presenting buyers of commercial libraries with alternative ecosystems that are free, interoperable and good enough (if not superior). MIP Optimization firms compete head-to-head in a growing market and so new entrants should consider carefully how they position themselves. Commercial firms now compete to find underserved customer algorithm needs (niche, cutting edge) and to add ease-of-use, breadth, performance, features or services to differentiate. In this fast-moving, highly competitive environment, it is hard to see how Porter’s concept of long-term sustainable advantage can be achieved. Indeed, the work of Rita Gunther McGrath is useful here. She argues that today firms must now prepare themselves to move through the stages of competitive advantage - launch, ramp up, exploitation, reconfiguration, and disengagement - much more quickly, looking to build and exploit a series of transient advantages in order to gain longer term advantage. “So defining where you want to compete, how you intend to win, and how you are going to move from advantage to advantage is critical.” This Five Forces Analysis is only a jumping off point. It is designed to help build an understanding of the nature and strength of the forces at play in the Numerical Libraries Industry. NAG team members can now take these forces into account as they decide where to dig further and start making the tough choices about who to target, where to compete and how to organize the value chain to create healthy returns.
justification: The insight is considered relevant and potentially valuable to company strategy.

description: Buyer Bargaining Power - Numerical libraries buyers are numerous, fragmented and varied. Ordinarily, this reduces leverage. However, buyers also have a lot of choice. There are numerous options to ‘do the same job’ in many areas of numerical libraries, many of them high quality and free. In these areas, the algorithms could be considered to be standard/undifferentiated. This increases buyer leverage. When it comes to core math libraries, most buyers will use free Intel MKL, NVIDIA CUDAx, AMD AOCL or purchase Arm Optimized Math Libraries, etc. as these libraries have access to propriety information that ensures best performance on their chips. In certain cases (e.g. Arm), the vendor may become a buyer/licensor of these libraries to offer to end users. In certain cases, finance buyers will deliberately minimise use of MKL and CUDAx to avoid (i) lock in (ii) allow easy switch between suppliers and architectures e.g. may want to run on CPU and GPU and so minimise MKL and CuDAx dependencies. This may be a hangover from the AMD Opteron days, but the behaviour is still there. Certain buyers have more leverage than others Government labs, academic institutions or major corporations who have large systems, buy site-wide licenses with many nodes Hardware and software vendors who can credibly threaten to vertically integrate libraries (chipmakers, hardware vendors, public cloud vendors, programming environment vendors) ISVs and Applications who serve as channels to end users Certain buyers have less leverage than others Buyers who have Code-bases with 3rd Party Dependencies- There is a subset of customers who have very large code bases with dependencies on 3rd parties (NAG, ISML,…) for whom migration would be expensive. Since their switching costs are high, these buyers are, in effect, locked in and have lower leverage. Buyers using integrated mathematical environments (e.g. MATLAB) where the user experience makes it easier to purchase vertically integrated algorithms (MATLAB toolboxes). Buyers operating in verticals where certain languages or programming environments are standard and used by the whole community (e.g. Computational Physics - Python, Automotive - MATLAB, CFD - OpenFOAM). Buyers requiring new or cutting-edge algorithms that are hard to build and where free alternatives of similar performance/quality do not exist (e.g. MILP optimization).

description: Discussion - Buyer Power - Numerical libraries are a component of the wider scientific computing industry. Buyers of scientific computing are from academic institutions, government labs and commercial firms. They come from a wide range of verticals. They purchase or use the scientific computing hardware, software and services offered by commercial vendors and open source communities to model and simulate complex real-world phenomena - e.g. financial portfolios, weather and climate, automobile safety, pharmaceutical drug discovery, transportation routes, and pricing. They do this through the use of numerical and statistical computing. The mathematical models of scientific computing rely on numerical analysis, and thus on a range of the algorithms that numerical libraries contain. Modelling and simulation are becoming more, not less, important to academics, governments and commercial firms today. Thus, HPC - the area of scientific computing that is well-tracked and documented - is growing, with overall HPC server revenues expected to grow from $13.76 billion in 2018 to $19.9 billion in 2020 (7.8% CAGR). We know that the fastest growing segment of this area has to do with high performance data analysis and AI, which will grow from $3.2 billion in 2018 to $6.4 billion in 2020 (15.4% CAGR). The AI-based HPC portion of this (mostly comprised of ML and DL related revenue) will grow at an even faster rate. Users of scientific computing have a few choices when it comes to how they incorporate the algorithms that power their models: Build from scratch - They can build from scratch - writing the algorithms themselves as they write the rest of their programs. This is not necessarily realistic for all numerical algorithms. IMSL has mapped the process of algorithm-creation on its new website and estimates that developing numerical algorithms in-house can take 8 weeks of development time plus 16 weeks of work associated with maintenance, porting, testing and documentation for a total of 24 weeks of dev time per in-house algorithm. Build with components - They can save time by calling established, tested algorithms from commercial or open source numerical libraries. Build with ‘tool-kits’ - They can use toolkits (e.g. PETSc), which typically include a grouping of algorithms, solvers and integrators that are then easy to use in application codes. Use readymade software (domain specific library, toolbox or applications) - They can use ready-made domain-specific applications, which are specifically designed for their use case, incorporating the algorithms and other programming they need to get them to their solution with less complexity or user skill (e.g. OpenFOAM, Abacus). Those who Build with Components form the group of potential buyers for Numerical Libraries. Toolkits and readymade software reduce buyers’ need to interact directly with Numerical Libraries; thus, they are Substitutes (discussed in the next section). As toolkits and readymade software become available for a wider range of domain-specific applications, buyers seem to be migrating towards these easier-to-use solutions, and the buyer group that chooses to primarily Build with Components seems to be narrowing. In 2019, Hyperion estimated the size of the HPC Middleware category (which includes numerical libraries) to be $1.58 billion in 2018, growing to $2.2 billion by 2023 (7% CAGR). The size of the Applications category is estimated to be somewhat larger, $4.6 billion in 2018 and growing to $6.4 billion by 2023 (CAGR 6.7%). In 2014, a survey by Intersect360 showed that MATLAB was the most used Middleware product. Intel MKL was near the middle of this list. In general, their survey also showed that there was a plethora of options for each use case (due to heavy focus of academic research on Middleware which resulted in open-source releases) and that respondents favoured open source over commercial by quite a lot. However, commercial buyers tended to prefer commercial vendors, valuing their product quality and service. This high number of (often-free) options per use case gives buyers more choice and, thus, increases their power. The following characteristics help determine the needs and preferences of NL buyers. These characteristics also help determine which libraries or substitutes are available for specific verticals and workloads, thus contributing to the leverage buyers have and the value they capture. Buyer Type - Are they from academia, government, or a commercial firm? This influences their goals, regulations, purchasing environment, and ways of working. Buyer System Size / Server Spending - How much are they spending on their system? Can be indicative of budgets and types/sizes of problems they are approaching. Buyer Vertical - Which vertical do they participate in and what workloads are they managing? Do these verticals have strong preferences for languages or software (e.g. MATLAB in engineering)? Buyer Algorithmic Approaches - Which algorithmic or computational approaches power their models (e.g. linear algebra, optimization, statistics, machine learning)? Buyer Geography - Are there geographical preferences, relationships, restrictions? Buyer Hardware - What hardware systems do they use (architecture, CPU, accelerator, memory, interconnect, storage, on-prem v. cloud)? Incompatible libraries are likely to be dismissed or phased out. Buyer Computing Language - What computing language(s) are they using? Is this changing? This helps determine the software ecosystem that they operate within and other libraries available to them. Buyer Software What software systems do they operate within (operating system, type of parallelism, development environment, age of code, etc.)? Libraries that integrate well with user software may gain an ease-of-use advantage, while buyers with aging code may end up ‘locked in’ to libraries used in the past. The tables below outline these buyer characteristics and attempt to quantify their importance (size / value / predicted growth / demand) where information is available.

description: Library developers - Library creation requires skilled mathematicians and statisticians who are increasingly in short supply. Often, they need good domain knowledge in a particular area of known/perceived strength combined with good technical skills. Sometimes, the ability to offer a certain function is dependent upon having access to a specialist in the area (AD/Optimization/FSI/O&G/HPC). Algorithm developer salaries, pensions, etc. are a costly factor (and according to Hyperion demand for individuals with these skills will only increase). Some firms may employ lower skilled staff to do parts of the job, though other tasks may need to be done by more technically skilled individuals. Some firms may also employ skilled staff from different geographic regions where salaries are lower (Intel MKL Russia, have heard of an investment bank doing so in Eastern Europe for quant finance). Licensed content Firms license some of their content from other entities (like Stanford) and pay royalty fees on it. Hardware vendors A good ecosystem of compilers and related tools are required to develop numerical libraries for regular hardware (CPUs). For CPUs there is a choice of tools/compilers (vendor provided and open source). For non-CPU (GPU, FPGA...), things are more complicated and often the numerical library write needs to reply on the vendor tools/compiler The hardware vendors previously discussed already offer core math libraries. They do pose a credible threat to further libraries integration in areas where it makes competitive sense for them. This is discussed in more detail in Threat of Entry and Rivals sections Software providers We have not identified powerful software providers at this time. Mathworks is an example of a software company that makes algorithm creation easier and that has also vertically integrated a wide range of numerical libraries.

description: No title provided - Industry: An industry is a group of firms producing products that are close substitutes for each other. Industries can be hard to define and are drawn upon product as well as geographic lines. For the purposes of this analysis, we assume that the NAG Library competes in the Numerical Libraries Industry, or more broadly the Math Software Industry. Library customers also participate in their own industries (Energy, Oil and Gas, Finance, Automotive, etc). These will be discussed as they relate to Buyer Power. The industry structure is developed from the perspective of a “business unit” which means a strategically independent part of the company’s offering. The Five Forces framework assumes that companies are structured with explicit business units, which is rarely the case for smaller companies such as NAG. However, it is essential that NAG’s strategically independent offerings are treated separately. For the purposes of this competitive analysis, we will define the following business units: NAG-L: NAG library and associated offerings, e.g. library-based consultancy (including Optimization) NAG-S: NAG technical and managed services [NAG-F: Financial Services Tools] - currently it is not clear if this should be considered separately

description: No title provided - The Fortran language, being highly suited to numerical and scientific computing has been the classic preferred language in the libraries industry and remains highly relevant across various subfields of the discipline. C, as the base language developed for UNIX, Linux and for tool developments such as compilers is both common and likely to remain important (not least because many higher-level languages such as Python and Ruby are written in C). Many customer segments use C++ as a primary workhorse language with vast ecosystems at the very least close integration with C++ as a result. Java, the most commonly used language in industry has evaded strong attention for numerical computation due to its innate inefficiencies due to non-native bytecode execution inside a virtual machine. However, most libraries (including NAG) do provide Java interfaces. During the 1990s and 2000s, MATLAB integrated programming environment corned the market on physical science and engineering disciplines and remains highly relevant in many of those fields today (e.g. mechanical engineering). However, many disciplines spanning engineering and computational physics have strongly favoured higher level languages such as Python due to the abstraction of scientific implementation from the underlying hardware details. As computers get more powerful, we expect more people to move to productivity-oriented environments like Python (as NAG saw users doing via the Hector contract). Pure Python tends to perform poorly. However, a well written scientific workflow is not in pure Python but uses Numpy as the basis. This offloads the heavy lifting to compiled libraries. Scipy, Scikit-learn, etc. all use Numpy as the fundamental basis. Library vendors such as Intel make use of this by providing versions of Numpy etc that are largely identical to use as the original but call into their optimised libraries. They can then provide extensions using a Numpy-like syntax that exposes the additional features of the vendor library. Intel’s RNGs are a great example of this. This is crucial because it means that if you write your Python workflow well it will execute just as quickly as the C/C++ equivalent but will be much cheaper to develop. Julia has been recognised as potentially useful for numerical computing, possessing both high-level OO attributes, but also creating native machine instructions allowing reasonable performance. However, despite growing popularity Julia remains a niche language. It would be great if we could predict which languages will dominate scientific computing in the next decade. We should perhaps split the languages into categories to attempt this prediction. For hardcore numerical programming Fortran and C/C++ will continue to dominate. Fortran remains because of the large number of legacy applications and will continue to decline slowly. C/C++ will attract most of the growth / new development and appears to be the language of choice for the accelerators (GPU, FPGA, ASICs as well as CPU). The author considers OpenCL, CUDA,… to be within the C++ category. For the ‘easier’ to use languages Python is hot right now and has so much momentum it will be here for the next decade for sure. There has also been a lot of activity around efficient Just In Time (JIT) compilation for Python which can improve the performance of native Python substantially (Numba in particular, which NAG teaches via Mike C’s High Performance Python course). Python will continue to link into compiled languages/libraries for speed. As for the rest it is much harder to predict. Julia continues grow, but what other new languages will emerge (Rust, .NET (F#/C#) increase as it is no longer a Windows only language due to .NETcore,..)
justification: The insight is considered relevant and potentially valuable to company strategy.

description: HPC Still Growing - According to Hyperion Research, HPC adoption by companies of all sizes - small, medium and large - has helped expand global HPC spending from 2 billion in 1990 to £24 billion in 2017 to an anticipated £38 billion in 2022 (£19.6 billion from servers; £18.4 billion from storage, software and support). The user base in that time has expanded from almost exclusively government and academic entities to one that is half comprised of private sector businesses, and in general, the number of HPC systems out there has increased - with a total of 88,600 systems sold across all size/price bands in 2017. Half of the revenues and 81,400 of the systems sold in 2017 were in the sub-£250,000 Workgroup and Departmental price bands - showing that the use of scientific and high performance computing has extended into the level of small-medium enterprises and workgroup/departments of large firms. Buyers of HPC across a wide range of sectors report that they could no longer compete without it and that their strategies to out-compete each other now include to out-compute each other. A Hyperion study found that many buyers of HPC report high ROI per £1 of investment in HPC.
justification: The insight is considered relevant and potentially valuable to company strategy.

description: Key Findings - This force is strong in the Numerical Libraries Industry - with free vendor libraries and free opensource ecosystems handing much value to buyers at the expense of commercial libraries. “Hardware vendors can create high-performing libraries for whatever user group they choose to target. Indeed, one could argue that users EXPECT hardware vendors to supply a certain set of libraries these days, which means that hardware vendors MUST create numerical libraries. As they compete for cloud space, this need will likely be higher.” The Python and Julia languages and their ecosystems are now providing free, comprehensive, highly performant libraries with permissive licenses to rival most of the rest. MATLAB has managed to capture quite a lot of value from its libraries through differentiation - by targeting industries that typically don’t use open source, taking a customer solutions approach, using an innovative pay per toolkit model, and continuously adding new features/compatibility to its large ecosystem to stay ahead. The Simulink product seems to shield against Python and Julia for certain client bases - for now. Commercial numerical libraries are numerous and have their fair share of open source competition. Commercial libraries differentiate on stability, performance, support, breadth and/or specialization to specific languages (e.g. .NET), verticals (e.g. Finance) or routines. Information available for comparing these libraries seems to be low, requiring user research and experimentation. MIP optimization is one area where there is a large performance gap between open source and commercial solvers; thus, there is still value to be captured by commercial firms. Here, the rivalry is intense with four firms in direct competition, at least two of which have stated goals to gain market share. This will lead to competitive battles and potentially to expansion of the market (Gartner report - only 10% of demand satisfied).
justification: The insight is considered relevant and potentially valuable to company strategy.

description: Quantum computing instead of numerical computing - Quantum computing systems have the potential to exceed the performance of conventional computers for cybersecurity, materials science, chemistry, pharmaceuticals, machine learning and optimization. They are not likely to replace conventional computing entirely, but they may become a substitute for certain classes of problem which can handle the difficulties currently associated with quantum computing and which benefit from a massive speed-up in performance. Right now, the technical challenges are still quite large and the time horizons are unclear. The algorithms and applications landscape is described as a wild west, and it is now thought that users will have to deal with an initial noisy period - where applications will have to tolerate/work around a lot of noise. Applications that lend themselves well to operating in a noisy environment could include optimization for portfolios, customer affinity or chemical reactions. The time horizon is still very uncertain. Most nations who commonly use HPC are funding quantum research -China and US are putting in the most, followed by Germany. It sounds like quantum computers will use quantum numerical algorithms (quantum simulation, eigenvalue estimation, integration, partial differential equations, and numerical linear algebra problems) to solve computational science problems, so it could be that this is a new hardware to develop for, rather than a substitute. It is important to note that quantum will be unsuited to data intensive processing, as data access cost grows exponentially with data size.
justification: The insight is considered relevant and potentially valuable to company strategy.

description: Discussion - Threat of New Entrants - In the Numerical Libraries industry, the threat of entry depends on the portion of the library that is being considered. When considering the vast scope that the NAG Library covered, the threat of specific entry into provision of similar functionality is almost zero, requiring vast and diverse skillsets and decades of development effort. However, the threat of entry is not a general one but a targeted one - an entrant could develop a new solution tailored to the needs of a specific customer segment that is underserved by the existing solutions. This is a realistic threat of entry, for which the industry has seen several precedents, including fundamental Linear Algebra, Optimisation and Machine Learning (traditional and deep learning). In virtually every area of general numerical libraries, you can find an organization that has gone specialist. Intel and NVIDIA vertically integrated a certain subset of performance-related libraries, starting in 2003 and approximately 2010 respectively. They have put their considerable resources behind becoming the leading providers of BLAS, LAPACK, FFT, Random Number Generators, etc. for their hardware, garnering large userbases. NVIDIA’s HPC Software development kit contains the compilers, libraries (BLAS, LAPACK, FFT, Sparse, RNG, LAPACK, Tensor), and software tools to increase developer productivity and performance on NVIDIA GPUS. Intel’s MKL library is now the benchmark on which other libraries are judged in these specific areas of fundamental linear algebra, FFTs and random number generation. Gurobi is an example of a new entrant into the optimization solver space in the last 12 years (2008). The founder of CPLEX and former lead developer for CPLEX left to create a competing optimization library. Since their business is based upon delivering the highest performance optimization library, they now spend large budgets on R&D to maintain their advantage. In both cases, the barriers to entry have been high, due to technical expertise and the accessibility of academic literature. Intel have employed a very large MKL development team in Russia for a considerable period to add hand-tuned x86 and SSE/AVX codes in assembly language, in addition to a reasonable development outfit in their Oregon offices. Gurobi have hired what they call “the most experienced development team in the industry” and took about 2 to 3 years to build a competitive product. decade In the case of Intel or NVIDIA, the value-add that is provided by the presence of MKL or CUDA is hard to measure but almost certainly of net benefit. In the case of Gurobi, the entrant has walked into a classic rivalry for market share amongst fit competitors, and it is not clear if the company yet possesses a sustainable advantage, despite being more focused than the competitors. Academics regularly collaborate with industry to advance algorithmic content, often publishing open sources versions of libraries created as a part of their research. These contribute to the body of competing free algorithms - capping prices and presenting competitors and potential entrants with reusable resources. Firms like Microsoft, Amazon and Google are currently racing to gain a share of the emerging HPC Cloud business. We understand that all are hiring from HPC to build HPC programming environments on the Cloud. This is leading the cloud vendors to build richer ecosystems for their users, which will almost certainly include some form of libraries. They will use the vendors codes, but also plug gaps through their own initiatives and acquisition. One of the best-known examples of a Cloud Service Provider (CSP) writing math functions is Google’s Ceres Solver (non-linear optimization solver). FPGA providers have traditionally had weak or no math libraries (or related library building tools - compilers etc) however in the last 3 years they have addressed this in order to target traditional compute workloads displacing CPUs & GPUs as the compute architecture or choice. Xillinx (FPGA manufacturer) is providing numerical libraries for its hardware as is Intel (Altera).
justification: The insight is considered relevant and potentially valuable to company strategy.

description: Advanced Data Analytics & AI - It must be noted that some of the new interest in scientific and high-performance computing is driven by the growing importance to commercial, academic and government sectors of emerging high-performance analytics methods (which Hyperion terms HPDA, High Performance Data Analysis). HPDA combines long-standing methods of data-intensive modelling and simulation with newer high-performance analytic methods - large-scale graph analytics, semantic technologies, and knowledge discovery algorithms. These HPDA methods will be used to support some of the highest value use cases in HPC going forward - autonomous vehicles, precision medicine, smart cities and the Internet of Things, all of which are extensions of activities that scientific computing and HPC have long supported - vehicle design, health care, urban transportation, regional/national power grids, and large distributed networks. This powerful combination of HPC with Advanced Analytics and AI is widely acknowledged and rivals are moving to develop their offerings in this direction. Intel and NVIDIA have introduced Data Analytics libraries and MATLAB has released toolboxes to extend engineers into Machine Learning / AI. NVIDIA advertises: HPC and AI are converging to extend the reach of science and accelerate the pace of scientific innovation. With AI, HPC is tackling previously unsolvable problems by modelling the world using experimental and simulation data. It’s also delivering real-time results with models that used to take days or months to simulate.
justification: The insight is considered relevant and potentially valuable to company strategy.

description: Vendor Libraries Gain Importance - Historically, hardware vendors consistently developed numerical libraries containing programs specifically optimised for the latest hardware releases, in order to provide additional value to their customers. This was the case for system-level providers (IBM, Cray, SGI, Fujitsu, NEC) but also from chip providers themselves (Intel, DEC). During this period, Moore’s law guaranteed performance improvements between successive chip and system generations. In the early 2000s, due to the end of Moore’s law and the emergence of e.g. multi-core chips, performance improvements became increasingly more difficult to obtain, requiring more investment into software on the part of hardware vendors. Chip vendors like Intel began to increasingly see the software stack / programming environment as a key factor in exploiting the performance of their systems and, thus, in their ability to differentiate/compete against their own rivals. Intel released its Math Kernel Library in 2003 to provide BLAS, LAPACK, ScaLAPACK, sparse solvers, FFTs and vector math. AMD responded with a similar product (ACML). In the following period, Intel’s massive investment established MKL as the industry leader in terms of free content, but also the benchmark by which competitors would be judged in terms of performance. This quickly drove many systems and chip providers to drop library developments in favour of using the CPU provided libraries. The only system provider that develops a comprehensive core math library offering today is Cray (now HPE). The trend of increasing core count to provide performance improvements has continued. Further, the cost of performing memory operations has become very expensive relative to that of performing arithmetic. The result is that the software stack has increasingly become seen as the key differentiator by the hardware vendors, who significantly increased investment in Software R&D. Around 2010, Graphics Processing Units began to be used as scientific program accelerators. By 2011 the world’s fastest computers used NVIDIA GPUs. GPUs required even greater degree of code customisation and effort in order for programmers to obtain reasonable performance, and so companies like NVIDIA (and later AMD) began investing heavily in providing custom programming environments. Today NVIDIA is the leader in terms of software innovation in both HPC and in vendor supplied numerical libraries, buoyed by the commercial success of GPUs for deep learning. On CPU (x86) Intel is the dominant provider of CPUs and it has the strongest core math libraries. description: Document Root - Numerical Libraries Industry - Industry Evolution - Languages. The Fortran language, being highly suited to numerical and scientific computing has been the classic preferred language in the libraries industry and remains highly relevant across various subfields of the discipline. C, as the base language developed for UNIX, Linux and for tool developments such as compilers is both common and likely to remain important (not least because many higher-level languages such as Python and Ruby are written in C). Many customer segments use C++ as a primary workhorse language with vast ecosystems at the very least close integration with C++ as a result. Java, the most commonly used language in industry has evaded strong attention for numerical computation due to its innate inefficiencies due to non-native bytecode execution inside a virtual machine. However, most libraries (including NAG) do provide Java interfaces. During the 1990s and 2000s, MATLAB integrated programming environment corned the market on physical science and engineering disciplines and remains highly relevant in many of those fields today (e.g. mechanical engineering). However, many disciplines spanning engineering and computational physics have strongly favoured higher level languages such as Python due to the abstraction of scientific implementation from the underlying hardware details. As computers get more powerful, we expect more people to move to productivity-oriented environments like Python (as NAG saw users doing via the Hector contract). Pure Python tends to perform poorly. However, a well written scientific workflow is not in pure Python but uses Numpy as the basis. This offloads the heavy lifting to compiled libraries. Scipy, Scikit-learn, etc. all use Numpy as the fundamental basis. Library vendors such as Intel make use of this by providing versions of Numpy etc that are largely identical to use as the original but call into their optimised libraries. They can then provide extensions using a Numpy-like syntax that exposes the additional features of the vendor library. Intel’s RNGs are a great example of this. This is crucial because it means that if you write your Python workflow well it will execute just as quickly as the C/C++ equivalent but will be much cheaper to develop. Julia has been recognised as potentially useful for numerical computing, possessing both high-level OO attributes, but also creating native machine instructions allowing reasonable performance. However, despite growing popularity Julia remains a niche language. It would be great if we could predict which languages will dominate scientific computing in the next decade. We should perhaps split the languages into categories to attempt this prediction. For hardcore numerical programming Fortran and C/C++ will continue to dominate. Fortran remains because of the large number of legacy applications and will continue to decline slowly. C/C++ will attract most of the growth / new development and appears to be the language of choice for the accelerators (GPU, FPGA, ASICs as well as CPU). The author considers OpenCL, CUDA,… to be within the C++ category. For the ‘easier’ to use languages Python is hot right now and has so much momentum it will be here for the next decade for sure. There has also been a lot of activity around efficient Just In Time (JIT) compilation for Python which can improve the performance of native Python substantially (Numba in particular, which NAG teaches via Mike C’s High Performance Python course). Python will continue to link into compiled languages/libraries for speed. As for the rest it is much harder to predict. Julia continues grow, but what other new languages will emerge (Rust, .NET (F#/C#) increase as it is no longer a Windows only language due to .NETcore,..)

description: Document Root - Numerical Libraries Five Forces - Conclusion. The wider scientific computing industry is booming - with server sales growing, cloud usage growing, compute speeds and storage capacities growing, and demand for simulation, optimization and HPDA/AI expanding to more of the enterprise segment (as well as academic and government). At the same time, the commercial software landscape is becoming ever more difficult to navigate - as hardware vendors increasingly offer components (including libraries) for free and open source ecosystems reach an unprecedented level of maturity. The forces that shape the Numerical Libraries Industry are not benign and have changed over time. The Threat of New Entrants is High - This threat is present and continual. It has caused erosion in the past and will do so in the future, fuelled by hardware and cloud vendor rivalries, by open source contributors (academics, students and government labs, often with financial contributions from industry), and by skilled developers launching new commercial offerings. The Bargaining Power of Suppliers is Moderate What next and algorithms suppliers (academic and government collaborators, algorithm developers) offer a credible threat to forward integrate - by offering free libraries, releasing new open source libraries, or launching new commercial libraries businesses. There is, however, a large number of suppliers which reduces their overall power. The Bargaining Power of Buyers is High - They now capture a lot of the value and have come to expect much libraries content to come for free. They have an increasing selection of free open source options to choose from, and they can turn to substitutes (some of which are also free) to satisfy their needs. Customers with code-base dependencies or other specialised needs have reduced leverage. Firms must introduce features, improve performance, adapt to new technology, specialize or meet risk/regulatory requirements to differentiate. The Threat of Substitution is Moderate-High - Toolkits and readymade software (some of which are, again, free) substitute the need to build with numerical libraries. While deep learning may replace numerical libraries in certain areas, it is likely that machine learning, deep learning and traditional numerical libraries will need to work together in the future, so compatibility will become important. Rivalry Among Existing Competitors is High - Vendors are engaged in their own rivalry for dominance in shifting chip and cloud industries. Python and Julia are eroding industry value overall, challenging the competitive equilibrium of Integrated Math Engines like Mathworks, and presenting buyers of commercial libraries with alternative ecosystems that are free, interoperable and good enough (if not superior). MIP Optimization firms compete head-to-head in a growing market and so new entrants should consider carefully how they position themselves. Commercial firms now compete to find underserved customer algorithm needs (niche, cutting edge) and to add ease-of-use, breadth, performance, features or services to differentiate. In this fast-moving, highly competitive environment, it is hard to see how Porter’s concept of long-term sustainable advantage can be achieved. Indeed, the work of Rita Gunther McGrath is useful here. She argues that today firms must now prepare themselves to move through the stages of competitive advantage - launch, ramp up, exploitation, reconfiguration, and disengagement - much more quickly, looking to build and exploit a series of transient advantages in order to gain longer term advantage. “So defining where you want to compete, how you intend to win, and how you are going to move from advantage to advantage is critical.” This Five Forces Analysis is only a jumping off point. It is designed to help build an understanding of the nature and strength of the forces at play in the Numerical Libraries Industry. NAG team members can now take these forces into account as they decide where to dig further and start making the tough choices about who to target, where to compete and how to organize the value chain to create healthy returns.

description: Document Root - Numerical Libraries Five Forces - Power of Buyers - Discussion - Buyer Power. Numerical libraries are a component of the wider scientific computing industry. Buyers of scientific computing are from academic institutions, government labs and commercial firms. They come from a wide range of verticals. They purchase or use the scientific computing hardware, software and services offered by commercial vendors and open source communities to model and simulate complex real-world phenomena - e.g. financial portfolios, weather and climate, automobile safety, pharmaceutical drug discovery, transportation routes, and pricing. They do this through the use of numerical and statistical computing. The mathematical models of scientific computing rely on numerical analysis, and thus on a range of the algorithms that numerical libraries contain. Modelling and simulation are becoming more, not less, important to academics, governments and commercial firms today. Thus, HPC - the area of scientific computing that is well-tracked and documented - is growing, with overall HPC server revenues expected to grow from $13.76 billion in 2018 to $19.9 billion in 2020 (7.8% CAGR). We know that the fastest growing segment of this area has to do with high performance data analysis and AI, which will grow from $3.2 billion in 2018 to $6.4 billion in 2020 (15.4% CAGR). The AI-based HPC portion of this (mostly comprised of ML and DL related revenue) will grow at an even faster rate. Users of scientific computing have a few choices when it comes to how they incorporate the algorithms that power their models: Build from scratch - They can build from scratch - writing the algorithms themselves as they write the rest of their programs. This is not necessarily realistic for all numerical algorithms. IMSL has mapped the process of algorithm-creation on its new website and estimates that developing numerical algorithms in-house can take 8 weeks of development time plus 16 weeks of work associated with maintenance, porting, testing and documentation for a total of 24 weeks of dev time per in-house algorithm. Build with components - They can save time by calling established, tested algorithms from commercial or open source numerical libraries. Build with ‘tool-kits’ - They can use toolkits (e.g. PETSc), which typically include a grouping of algorithms, solvers and integrators that are then easy to use in application codes. Use readymade software (domain specific library, toolbox or applications) - They can use ready-made domain-specific applications, which are specifically designed for their use case, incorporating the algorithms and other programming they need to get them to their solution with less complexity or user skill (e.g. OpenFOAM, Abacus). Those who Build with Components form the group of potential buyers for Numerical Libraries. Toolkits and readymade software reduce buyers’ need to interact directly with Numerical Libraries; thus, they are Substitutes (discussed in the next section). As toolkits and readymade software become available for a wider range of domain-specific applications, buyers seem to be migrating towards these easier-to-use solutions, and the buyer group that chooses to primarily Build with Components seems to be narrowing. In 2019, Hyperion estimated the size of the HPC Middleware category (which includes numerical libraries) to be $1.58 billion in 2018, growing to $2.2 billion by 2023 (7% CAGR). The size of the Applications category is estimated to be somewhat larger, $4.6 billion in 2018 and growing to $6.4 billion by 2023 (CAGR 6.7%). In 2014, a survey by Intersect360 showed that MATLAB was the most used Middleware product. Intel MKL was near the middle of this list. In general, their survey also showed that there was a plethora of options for each use case (due to heavy focus of academic research on Middleware which resulted in open-source releases) and that respondents favoured open source over commercial by quite a lot. However, commercial buyers tended to prefer commercial vendors, valuing their product quality and service. This high number of (often-free) options per use case gives buyers more choice and, thus, increases their power. The following characteristics help determine the needs and preferences of NL buyers. These characteristics also help determine which libraries or substitutes are available for specific verticals and workloads, thus contributing to the leverage buyers have and the value they capture. Buyer Type - Are they from academia, government, or a commercial firm? This influences their goals, regulations, purchasing environment, and ways of working. Buyer System Size / Server Spending - How much are they spending on their system? Can be indicative of budgets and types/sizes of problems they are approaching. Buyer Vertical - Which vertical do they participate in and what workloads are they managing? Do these verticals have strong preferences for languages or software (e.g. MATLAB in engineering)? Buyer Algorithmic Approaches - Which algorithmic or computational approaches power their models (e.g. linear algebra, optimization, statistics, machine learning)? Buyer Geography - Are there geographical preferences, relationships, restrictions? Buyer Hardware - What hardware systems do they use (architecture, CPU, accelerator, memory, interconnect, storage, on-prem v. cloud)? Incompatible libraries are likely to be dismissed or phased out. Buyer Computing Language - What computing language(s) are they using? Is this changing? This helps determine the software ecosystem that they operate within and other libraries available to them. Buyer Software What software systems do they operate within (operating system, type of parallelism, development environment, age of code, etc.)? Libraries that integrate well with user software may gain an ease-of-use advantage, while buyers with aging code may end up ‘locked in’ to libraries used in the past. The tables below outline these buyer characteristics and attempt to quantify their importance (size / value / predicted growth / demand) where information is available.

description: Document Root - Numerical Libraries Five Forces - Threat of Substitutes - Discussion - Threat of Substitutes. The mathematical models of scientific computing rely on various types of numerical analysis/algorithms, and the importance of scientific computing is only increasing for academics, governments and commercial firms. Therefore, it must be said that numerical computing and the need for numerical libraries are not likely to go away soon. However, there may be ways in which buyers of scientific computing can get to their solution without accessing numerical libraries. Substitutes to consider are: Machine Learning - Deep Learning instead of Simulation or Optimization Machine Learning employs “algorithms that parse data, learn from that data, and then apply what they’ve learned to make informed decisions.” Machine Learning can be separated into two sub-fields, both of which fall under the broader category of AI - Deep Learning - neural nets combined with Big Data and GPUs. Structures algorithm in layers to create an “artificial neural network” that can learn and make decisions on its own; Traditional Machine Learning - pretty much all of ML except Deep Learning. Clustering, Classification, Regression and Market Basket Analysis. Traditional Machine Learning is the foundation for deep learning and has been around for decades. According to a 2019 Oracle overview blog, “most of what’s being applied today is traditional.” Hyperion Research estimates that both Traditional Machine Learning and Deep Learning will grow at a nearly 30 percent compound annual growth rate over the 2018 to 2023 period. Here we do see that ML is predicted to make up a larger share of the market than deep learning during this time. Questions about Machine Learning as a Substitute include, for example 1) whether Deep Learning will start to replace Traditional Machine Learning or simulation; and 2) whether Deep Learning will be used to eliminate the need for Optimization. We need help from those more familiar with Machine Learning to determine this. NVIDIA mentioned in 2016 that Generative Adversarial Networks might be one technology to watch that could replace traditional simulation. According to Jacques, “In finance we're seeing DL replacing "traditional" valuation methods such as PDEs or MC. We're even seeing it start to replace calibration (optimisation + interpolation). When I say "replace" I mean replace in the on-line calculation phase, i.e. day-to-day running of the bank. It's still needed for the offline phase where the models are trained. There is a strong incentive in the finance industry for this technology to work. The more they can replace with DNNs, the faster and cheaper they can do things. It can affect their hardware requirements massively, and hence their costs. I should add: FSI's use of DNNs is rather different from many other industries. They are approximating a complicated, but known deterministic function. With enough compute power (and patience), they can build a DNN once to compute that function to almost any level of accuracy.” Gurobi CEO states that he sees Machine/Deep Learning and Optimization working in concert - firms will use ML to make predictions about what is likely to happen in the business in the future and then will take those predictions and use Optimization (MIP in particular) to make recommendations about what which actions to take. This is likely a bit of marketing spin and/or an attempt by Gurobi to position optimization and deep learning as complements to one another. Jan and John expect that Gurobi will continue to provide just the MIP solver and are investigating possible ways to use/spin machine/deep learning at this time. It seems that Machine Learning, Deep Learning and simulation in general will be expected to work together in the future, so compatibility of traditional numerical algorithms with deep learning will become important. According to Hyperion Research, the algorithms that exist for HPDA and AI (ML/DL) are characteristic of an emerging field - not quite adequate for the future and not well classified. Other firms such as Univa, AWS, and Intel describe Machine Learning/AI and HPC as a wild west, with many algorithms that do the same thing and many areas unclear. This area of computing is emerging, with many standards still undefined.

description: Document Root - Numerical Libraries Five Forces - Threat of New Entrants - Discussion - Threat of New Entrants. In the Numerical Libraries industry, the threat of entry depends on the portion of the library that is being considered. When considering the vast scope that the NAG Library covered, the threat of specific entry into provision of similar functionality is almost zero, requiring vast and diverse skillsets and decades of development effort. However, the threat of entry is not a general one but a targeted one - an entrant could develop a new solution tailored to the needs of a specific customer segment that is underserved by the existing solutions. This is a realistic threat of entry, for which the industry has seen several precedents, including fundamental Linear Algebra, Optimisation and Machine Learning (traditional and deep learning). In virtually every area of general numerical libraries, you can find an organization that has gone specialist. Intel and NVIDIA vertically integrated a certain subset of performance-related libraries, starting in 2003 and approximately 2010 respectively. They have put their considerable resources behind becoming the leading providers of BLAS, LAPACK, FFT, Random Number Generators, etc. for their hardware, garnering large userbases. NVIDIA’s HPC Software development kit contains the compilers, libraries (BLAS, LAPACK, FFT, Sparse, RNG, LAPACK, Tensor), and software tools to increase developer productivity and performance on NVIDIA GPUS. Intel’s MKL library is now the benchmark on which other libraries are judged in these specific areas of fundamental linear algebra, FFTs and random number generation. Gurobi is an example of a new entrant into the optimization solver space in the last 12 years (2008). The founder of CPLEX and former lead developer for CPLEX left to create a competing optimization library. Since their business is based upon delivering the highest performance optimization library, they now spend large budgets on R&D to maintain their advantage. In both cases, the barriers to entry have been high, due to technical expertise and the accessibility of academic literature. Intel have employed a very large MKL development team in Russia for a considerable period to add hand-tuned x86 and SSE/AVX codes in assembly language, in addition to a reasonable development outfit in their Oregon offices. Gurobi have hired what they call “the most experienced development team in the industry” and took about 2 to 3 years to build a competitive product. decade In the case of Intel or NVIDIA, the value-add that is provided by the presence of MKL or CUDA is hard to measure but almost certainly of net benefit. In the case of Gurobi, the entrant has walked into a classic rivalry for market share amongst fit competitors, and it is not clear if the company yet possesses a sustainable advantage, despite being more focused than the competitors. Academics regularly collaborate with industry to advance algorithmic content, often publishing open sources versions of libraries created as a part of their research. These contribute to the body of competing free algorithms - capping prices and presenting competitors and potential entrants with reusable resources. Firms like Microsoft, Amazon and Google are currently racing to gain a share of the emerging HPC Cloud business. We understand that all are hiring from HPC to build HPC programming environments on the Cloud. This is leading the cloud vendors to build richer ecosystems for their users, which will almost certainly include some form of libraries. They will use the vendors codes, but also plug gaps through their own initiatives and acquisition. One of the best-known examples of a Cloud Service Provider (CSP) writing math functions is Google’s Ceres Solver (non-linear optimization solver). FPGA providers have traditionally had weak or no math libraries (or related library building tools - compilers etc) however in the last 3 years they have addressed this in order to target traditional compute workloads displacing CPUs & GPUs as the compute architecture or choice. Xillinx (FPGA manufacturer) is providing numerical libraries for its hardware as is Intel (Altera).

description: Document Root - Numerical Libraries Five Forces - Threat of Substitutes - Discussion - Threat of Substitutes - Quantum computing instead of numerical computing. Quantum computing systems have the potential to exceed the performance of conventional computers for cybersecurity, materials science, chemistry, pharmaceuticals, machine learning and optimization. They are not likely to replace conventional computing entirely, but they may become a substitute for certain classes of problem which can handle the difficulties currently associated with quantum computing and which benefit from a massive speed-up in performance. Right now, the technical challenges are still quite large and the time horizons are unclear. The algorithms and applications landscape is described as a wild west, and it is now thought that users will have to deal with an initial noisy period - where applications will have to tolerate/work around a lot of noise. Applications that lend themselves well to operating in a noisy environment could include optimization for portfolios, customer affinity or chemical reactions. The time horizon is still very uncertain. Most nations who commonly use HPC are funding quantum research -China and US are putting in the most, followed by Germany. It sounds like quantum computers will use quantum numerical algorithms (quantum simulation, eigenvalue estimation, integration, partial differential equations, and numerical linear algebra problems) to solve computational science problems, so it could be that this is a new hardware to develop for, rather than a substitute. It is important to note that quantum will be unsuited to data intensive processing, as data access cost grows exponentially with data size.

description: Document Root - Industry Structure Analysis - What is an Industry Structure (Five Forces) Analysis? . Michael Porter’s Five Forces Analysis is a framework to analyse and understand the structure of an industry. Industry structure is shaped by five key forces - threat of entry, power of suppliers, power of buyers, threat of substitute products or services, and intensity of rivalry among existing competitors. These forces have a strong influence in determining the environment in which firms compete - the rules of the game and the possible strategies available to a given firm. They play a large part in defining the profit potential of an industry (that is, how much value is created) and which parties in the industry capture those profits. Thus, the Five Forces Analysis is a great place to start the strategy development process. It helps us ensure that we are looking at the whole arena (not just competitors or buyers, but all five forces) when we formulate our approach. By understanding where forces are most intense/relevant, NAG Executives can determine where to focus further research and, ultimately, how to compete.

description: Document Root - Numerical Libraries Five Forces - Rivalry Among Existing Competitors - Discussion - Hardware Vendor Libraries . Hardware vendors provide free “fast as stink” core math libraries in order to ensure user performance on their hardware and thus sell more of it. These include BLAS, LAPACK, ScaLAPACK, sparse solvers, fast Fourier transforms, vector math, RNGs and some Partial Differential Equations. Some vendors have extended into data analytics and machine learning/AI libraries as well. Today, hardware vendors dominate core math libraries, as they possess the proprietary information to make the libraries perform better on their hardware, and they also maintain direct distribution channels to users. Due to the widespread usage of these fast core math libraries, the profit potential in this area of libraries is low. For hardware firms, these libraries are a cost of doing business. Their rivalry is focused on competition for chip and other hardware sales. This group of firms now seems to be striving for market share and dominance in the emerging computing world, one in which: heterogenous processors will increasingly be the norm- CPUs (Intel, AMD, Arm, Marvell, Power), GPUs (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel), FPGAs (Xillinx, Intel) AI-specific silicon (Cerebras, Intel Habana, Graphcore, and many more) data processing and storage present both a challenge-to-be-solved and a revenue opportunity; more and more workloads are moving to the cloud (and thus cloud providers are growing as a major buying group); systems hardware vendors are consolidating (HPE/Cray); and Big Data, AI (especially ML) and HPC are expected to converge.

description: Document Root - Numerical Libraries Industry - Industry Evolution - HPC and the Software Stack Advance. In the 1980s and 1990s, the arrival of affordable, entry-level HPC systems allowed companies of varying sizes to begin using advanced computing. Firms like MathWorks and Mathematica commercialised integrated programming environments that were specialised for modelling, visualisation and simulation. In addition, in 1983 the GNU Project was launched as the inaugural project of the Free Software Movement. Funded in large part by industry disk sales and donations during the ‘80s and ‘90s, GNU released a number of free software tools - programming language GNU Octave, GNU Scientific Libraries, etc. The Open Source software movement was then launched in 1998. A number of numerical libraries have subsequently been released by academics and other groups under open source or free licenses, increasing the availability of no cost numerical libraries of varying stability and quality.

description: Document Root - Numerical Libraries Five Forces - Threat of New Entrants - Key Findings. Threat of entry into Numerical Libraries should be assessed on a segment by segment basis (e.g. core math libraries, optimization, statistics, etc.). An equally important alternative approach is to analyse the new entrants by their user-centric / domain offering (e.g. in finance look at quantLib, FinCad, etc) Threat of entry by hardware providers (cloud, chip, etc.) into core math libraries, data analysis, machine/deep learning is high. These firms have large amounts of capital and the incentive to vertically integrate libraries that are critical to user performance, thus, improving differentiation and hardware revenue. Threat of entry by academics producing open source algorithms is high. These are regularly shared with the community by academics. The above represents both a challenge and an opportunity for commercial library writers. Challenge: academics regularly add free, open source algorithms to the market, increasing competition and price sensitivity. Opportunity: commercial libraries gain access to cutting edge research without having to fund it themselves. They can then use their skill at commercializing libraries to deliver a better offering to buyers quickly. More comprehensive languages + ecosystems that “do the same job” as general libraries (e.g. Python and SciPy, MATLAB, Julia, Wolfram) are a feasible and ongoing threat, though they have higher barriers to entry and take longer to develop. We should be on the lookout for those that may be up and coming.

description: Document Root - Numerical Libraries Five Forces - Rivalry Among Existing Competitors - Discussion - Numerical Optimization Libraries . Numerical Optimization has become a major category in its own right and would probably benefit from its own industry analysis. A 2015 Gartner Report describes Optimization as follows: Optimization is a prescriptive analytics approach used to solve complex decision problems that involve conflicting objectives and constraints, making the best use of limited resources. There are three segments of optimization solutions — domain-specific optimization, optimization modelling platforms for skilled users to define a problem, and the optimization solvers that work together with these platforms to find the "best" solution. Awareness of optimization in corporate BI and analytics teams has been limited, but with increased awareness of the benefits, usage is growing rapidly, especially in embedded applications. The 2014 Optimization Platform market was estimated by Gartner to be $100 million, growing at 10% for 2015 (with the Applications market being many times greater, e.g. this report summary estimates the Route Optimization software market alone will reach $5 billion by 2023). Gartner also noted that the overall 2015 Optimization Solutions market was still in the emerging phase, with only about 10% of potential demand satisfied. The Solver market size was not estimated but is undoubtedly smaller. Gartner also specifies that the industry as a whole consists of hundreds of firms, most of which operate in the domain-specific optimization applications category. Firms like FICO and IBM offer both solvers and modelling platforms (which allow skilled users to define optimization models for a wide variety of business problems) and Gurobi, Knitro, Mosek and other open-source providers focus on delivering superior optimization solvers. Below is a graphic which demonstrates how the categories interact with each other. Obviously, our focus remains on the libraries/solver space; however, it is interesting to note the links and the value is created in the related Optimization Solutions categories. Hyperion notes that Numeric Optimization is an important algorithmic approach for HPDA and that users require different approaches - Continuous, Discrete and Stochastic. The table below summarizes a survey of user preferences by vertical. We perceive that there is a relatively fierce battle between Gurobi and IBM/Cplex as well as FICO to release faster, better solvers. This takes place on the fronts of securing the best of a limited optimization talent pool, competing to release faster and better solvers (to be the best), pricing discounts and multi-year deals, marketing (see Gurobi ads on competitor pages and link about switching costs), exploring the use of optimization alongside ML (Gurobi, this may be all spin), and capturing new markets (Gurobi - Thompson Street Capital funding focus on new markets and market share gain; Mosek - search for board members indicates interest in expanding business before sale).
